```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
big <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
```

DietView can attach a taxonomic lineage to every prey by querying the
[World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS)](https://www.marinespecies.org/). This
vignette shows how to run the lookup, how to read the log of how each prey was
matched, and how to freeze the result so that later runs need no network. The
lookup chunks are shown but not run, because they need the `worrms` package and
an internet connection. Everything else runs on the public ICES stomach-content
extract that ships with the package (ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES,
Copenhagen; extract distributed with the R package stomachr, Lindmark 2026; see
`?ices_diet`) and on its frozen lineage, `ices_lineage`.

```{r setup}
library(DietView)

# drop non-food items and nematodes (mostly parasites, not prey)
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]

spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",
  prey_name      = "prey_name",
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "year", "quarter")
)
```

## Why a lineage, and why unidentified records stay

DietView shows the diet at seven ranks, kingdom to species, by default. Your
records rarely carry all seven: identification often stops at a coarse rank.
In the ICES data, prey are recorded at every level WoRMS knows:

```{r ranks}
ids <- unique(stats::na.omit(dat$prey_aphia_id))
sort(table(ices_lineage$worms_rank[ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id %in% ids]), decreasing = TRUE)
```

Only some of these `r length(ids)` prey names are species. The others stop at a
genus, a family, or something as coarse as "Crustacea" (a subphylum) or
"Pisces" (a superclass). DietView never fills in the missing ranks. Below the
last rank reached, the record is shown as unidentified at that rank, so every
ring of the sunburst still holds all the records and adds up to 100%.

## Running the lookup

`dv_prepare(taxonomy = "worms")` calls `dv_taxonomy_worms()` once for each
distinct prey key, not once per record: here `r length(ids)` AphiaIDs for
`r big(nrow(dat))` records. Each record is keyed by its AphiaID when it has
one, and by its name otherwise.

```{r prepare, eval = FALSE}
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "worms")
prep
```

In the ICES data, the only records without an AphiaID are the unidentified
material, named "Unidentified material". That name would be sent to WoRMS as
a name, fail the exact match and go to fuzzy matching, which has nothing
useful to find. Remove the name from the lookup, so these records stay plainly
unidentified (`dv_prepare()` then warns that they have no key, which is what
you want):

```{r prepare-unid, eval = FALSE}
lookup <- dat
lookup$prey_name[lookup$item_type == "unidentified"] <- NA
prep <- dv_prepare(lookup, spec, taxonomy = "worms")
```

## How each prey is matched

Each distinct prey gets one row in the log, with a `match_type`:

| `match_type` | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | The AphiaID is accepted in WoRMS | Nothing, unless `name_check` is `"differs"` |
| `id_synonym` | The AphiaID is unaccepted; its accepted ID was used | Check that the accepted name is the taxon you meant |
| `id_unchecked` | WoRMS could not be reached to check the ID | Run again later |
| `exact` | No ID; the name matched exactly | Nothing |
| `fuzzy` | No ID; the name was matched by TAXAMATCH, which tolerates misspellings | Check every one: a near match can be a different taxon |
| `unresolved` | No match | Correct the name, or accept that the prey stays unidentified |

### Matching by AphiaID: `id` and `id_synonym`

Every ICES prey record carries an AphiaID, so a lookup on these data runs
almost entirely through the first two rows of the table. Most IDs are accepted
(`id`). Some are not. The frozen lineage shows two pairs of names that differ
by one letter:

```{r pairs}
pairs <- c("Aphrodita aculeata", "Aphrodite aculeata",
           "Trisopterus esmarkii", "Trisopterus esmarki")
lin_pairs <- ices_lineage[ices_lineage$scientific_name %in% pairs,
                          c("prey_aphia_id", "scientific_name", "family", "species")]
lin_pairs$n_records <- as.vector(table(dat$prey_aphia_id)[as.character(lin_pairs$prey_aphia_id)])
lin_pairs
table(dat$prey_name[dat$prey_name %in% pairs], dat$country[dat$prey_name %in% pairs])
```

Each pair is one species (a sea mouse and Norway pout) under two AphiaIDs, and
one spelling of each comes from a single country. WoRMS keeps variant
spellings like these as unaccepted names with AphiaIDs of their own. A live
lookup reads each AphiaID's record; when it is unaccepted, it follows it to the
accepted AphiaID, logs it as `id_synonym` and gives both spellings the same
lineage. The frozen
`ices_lineage` was built from the AphiaIDs as reported, so it keeps them
apart, and the species ring counts each species twice. It matters for any
species-level statement:

```{r split}
cod <- dat[dat$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ]
prep_cod <- dv_prepare(cod, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                       verbose = FALSE)
fo <- dv_fo_table(prep_cod, rank = "species")
fo[fo$taxon %in% pairs, ]
```

When you work offline, the same correction is one line per pair, made on your
copy of the data before `dv_prepare()`. Keep it in the script, so the change is
visible:

```{r merge}
accepted <- c("231869" = 129840L,   # Aphrodite aculeata  -> Aphrodita aculeata
              "400596" = 126444L)   # Trisopterus esmarki -> Trisopterus esmarkii
fix <- as.character(cod$prey_aphia_id) %in% names(accepted)
cod$prey_aphia_id[fix] <- accepted[as.character(cod$prey_aphia_id[fix])]
cod$prey_name[fix] <- ices_lineage$scientific_name[
  match(cod$prey_aphia_id[fix], ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
prep_cod <- dv_prepare(cod, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                       verbose = FALSE)
fo <- dv_fo_table(prep_cod, rank = "species")
fo[fo$taxon %in% pairs, ]
```

```{r merged, include = FALSE}
fo_split <- dv_fo_table(dv_prepare(dat[dat$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ], spec,
                                   taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                                   verbose = FALSE), rank = "species")
split_rank <- which(fo_split$taxon[fo_split$taxon != "NA"] == "Aphrodita aculeata")
sea_mouse <- fo[fo$taxon == "Aphrodita aculeata", ]
sea_rank  <- which(fo$taxon[fo$taxon != "NA"] == "Aphrodita aculeata")
```

Merged, the sea mouse is found in `r sea_mouse$n_stomachs` cod stomachs
(`r sea_mouse$pct_fo`%) and ranks number `r sea_rank` among the named species
of the cod diet by frequency of occurrence; split, its more common spelling
ranked number `r split_rank`.

`name_check` compares the name in your table with the name WoRMS holds for
the AphiaID. In `ices_diet` the prey names were taken from WoRMS by AphiaID, so
they agree by construction. In your own data, `"differs"` usually means that a
name or an ID was mistyped, and the two point to different taxa.

### Matching by name: `exact` and `fuzzy`

Names are used only when there is no AphiaID. To see what that path does, take
a few ICES prey names, one of them misspelled:

```{r names, eval = FALSE}
keys <- data.frame(prey_id   = NA,
                   prey_name = c("Crangon crangon", "Ammodytidae", "Crangon crangom"))
dv_taxonomy_worms(keys)
```

The first two names should come back as `exact`. The third fails the exact
match; with `fuzzy = TRUE`, WoRMS TAXAMATCH proposes the closest name it knows
and the row is logged as `fuzzy`, with the proposal in `matched_name`. For a
one-letter slip the proposal is usually the intended name, but a near match can
just as well be another taxon one letter away. Check every fuzzy row.

### The other columns of the log

`lineage_ok` is `FALSE` when the prey was matched but WoRMS returned no
classification, for example because the connection failed. Those prey count as
unidentified at every rank until you run the lookup again. Failed lookups are
not stored in the cache, so the next run asks WoRMS again. `names_seen` lists
every name found under one key: more than one name under the same AphiaID is
worth a look. `homonym` flags a name with several accepted WoRMS records.

Successful lookups are cached on disk (in `tools::R_user_dir("DietView", "cache")`),
so a rerun only queries what changed. The log also records when the taxonomy
was retrieved and which `worrms` version was used, in its `retrieved` and
`worrms_version` attributes.

## Reading the report

`dv_taxonomy_report()` returns the prey that need a look, largest number of
records first:

```{r report, eval = FALSE}
review <- dv_taxonomy_report(prep, which = "review")
review

# the whole log, to archive or to send to a co-author
dv_taxonomy_report(prep, which = "all", file = file.path(tempdir(), "taxonomy_log.csv"))
```

On the ICES data, the rows to expect there are unaccepted AphiaIDs
(`id_synonym`), with the number of records each one affects. Unresolved prey you did not
expect are the ones to chase.

## The frozen alternative: `ices_lineage`

A lineage table is the reproducible path: no network, no change between runs.
`ices_lineage` is one such table, with one row per AphiaID:

```{r frozen}
dim(ices_lineage)
ices_lineage[ices_lineage$scientific_name %in% c("Crangon crangon", "Ammodytidae",
                                                  "Crustacea", "Pisces"), ]
```

It was not produced by `dv_taxonomy_worms()`. It comes from the WoRMS
classification that the R package stomachr (Lindmark 2026) compiled for the
AphiaIDs of the ICES extract; the script `data-raw/ices_data.R` in the
package sources reshapes it into DietView's seven ranks. Two columns are
derived there rather than read from WoRMS: `kingdom`, from the phylum, and
`species`, from the name when its WoRMS rank is species or subspecies (a
subspecies is reported under its species). A name above species keeps only
the ranks WoRMS gives it, so "Crustacea" has a phylum and nothing below. It is
used with `taxonomy = "table"`; the key column `prey_aphia_id` has the same
name as the prey key of `ices_diet`:

```{r use-frozen}
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                   verbose = FALSE)
prep
```

A table path has no match log: the lineage is taken as given. `dv_prepare()`
warns if a prey key is missing from the table, and those records are kept as
unidentified at every rank.

## Correcting and freezing your own lookup

Fix the names or IDs the report lists in your source table and run the lookup
again. When the log is clean, save the lineage, keyed by the same column as
your data, and switch to the offline path for every later run:

```{r fix, eval = FALSE}
lineage <- unique(prep$data[, c(spec$prey_id, prep$ranks)])
lin_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "lineage_2026-10-20.csv")   # use your project folder
write.csv(lineage, lin_file, row.names = FALSE)

lineage <- read.csv(lin_file, na.strings = c("NA", ""))
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = lineage)
```

The lineage table fixes the taxonomic snapshot your figures were made from.
Archive it with your data, together with the log, and note the retrieval date
and the `worrms` version, because WoRMS changes.

## Exact matching only

To turn off TAXAMATCH matching and keep only known AphiaIDs and exact names:

```{r conservative, eval = FALSE}
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "worms", fuzzy = FALSE)
```
